I never went to school, but I've been farming these fields for 20 years and I know what works. My farm is almost 380 mu — way too much for four people to handle alone — so I hire workers for picking cotton, spraying, and running the irrigation. I have my own well, but pumping water costs diesel, so I don't irrigate more than I have to. Last year I planted about 300 mu of cotton and the rest in spring maize, and it paid off, so I'm doing the same this year. I don't trust new ideas unless my cousin or the big farmer down the road tries them first and shows me the results. Cotton is my main crop — it's what brings in the money.

For cotton, I sow in mid-April with variety 802, same seed my neighbor uses. His cotton always grows strong. I rotary till the land first — cotton needs a soft bed. At planting I put down about one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, roughly 30 kg, and when the plants start flowering I broadcast another topdressing of urea. I irrigate twice from my well, once at flowering and once when the bolls are filling. Pumping is expensive but if it doesn't rain the yield drops hard. I spray about 15 times total for insects and weeds — bollworm is my worst enemy. I hire a crop-dusting plane for the big fields and workers with backpack sprayers for the edges. I expect around 550 kg per mu, same as last year.

For maize, I plant hybrid Denghai 605 in early May. Half the village uses that seed and nobody complains. I rotary till that land too since it's spring maize — I have time, unlike summer maize after wheat where you have to rush. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and topdress with urea when the plants are knee-high. Two irrigations should do it, and I spray about four times total for insects and weeds. Maize is easier than cotton. If the weather holds, I should get about 1400 kg per mu.

I don't try to save money on fertilizer or water if it means risking the crop. A bad year hurts more than a good year helps, and I have workers to pay.
